issues.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is valid where the propounder proves its due execution and the testator’s capacity, and satisfactorily explains any suspicious circumstances surrounding it.
material_facts: The dispute arose in a partition suit in which the appellants challenged a will that excluded certain properties from partition.

The scribe testified that the testator dictated the will. Two attesting witnesses testified that the testator signed it in their presence while of sound mind, understood its dispositions, and that they attested it in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence.
A handwriting expert testified that the signatures on all six pages of the will were the testator’s signatures.
The testator was 80 years old and died 15 days after executing the will, but the scribe and attesting witnesses testified that he was in sound physical and mental condition.

The properties allotted to two sons in an earlier partition had been held by tenants and later vested in the government, while the properties given to those sons by the will had been in the testator’s personal cultivation; the will also provided other heirs with rights to compensation for the vested lands.

The evidence showed that the daughters were present when the will was executed and that its contents had been disclosed at the testator’s final obeisance ceremony and during proceedings before forest authorities.

The will was registered four years after execution; the respondents explained that they did so on legal advice, and the scribe and attesting witnesses gave consistent accounts before the registrar and in court.
The evidence did not establish that a respondent’s presence in the house amounted to a prominent role in execution of the will.
issues.conclusion: The propounders proved that the will was duly executed by a testator of sound disposing mind, and the circumstances relied on to challenge it did not prevent its acceptance as genuine and valid. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will requires the prescribed attestation. The propounder bears the burden of proving due execution, testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature; where suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction. If undue influence, fraud or coercion is alleged, the person making that allegation bears the burden of proving it. Proof is assessed by the satisfaction of a prudent mind, and suspicious circumstances depend on the facts of the particular case. The court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma; Ramachandra Rambux v. Champabai; Surendra Pal v. Dr. (Mrs.) Saraswati Arora; Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. Smt. Amrit Kaur; and Meenakshiammal v. Chandrasekaran.

rule.if: partition_suit_appeal_challenging_will and testamentary_execution_proved and testamentary_capacity_proved and (not suspicious_circumstances_present or suspicious_circumstances_explained)

predicates.partition_suit_appeal_challenging_will: A party in an appeal arising from a partition suit challenges the validity of a will affecting which property is available for partition.
predicates.testamentary_execution_proved: The propounder establishes that the testator signed the will and that the required witnesses attested it in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence.
predicates.testamentary_capacity_proved: Evidence establishes that, when signing the will, the testator was of sound disposing mind and understood the nature and effect of its dispositions.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_present: Facts surrounding the will raise circumstances that could reasonably cast doubt on its genuine execution.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_explained: The propounder gives evidence that satisfactorily accounts for the circumstances capable of casting doubt on the will.

issues.definition: When a will is challenged in an appeal arising from a partition suit, proof of its execution and the testator’s capacity, together with a satisfactory explanation of any suspicious circumstances, results in the will being accepted as genuine and valid.
